extracted.intended_audience: scientists, philosophers of science, and advanced students of scientific method
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for judging scientific knowledge: distinguishing empirical facts from explanations, assessing the role of accident, and testing theories by prediction and deduction. Focuses on what makes a satisfactory explanation, how theory and experiment interact, and the evidential value of predictive success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish empirical collections from theoretical laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Many branches of knowledge consist of mere collections of disconnected empirical facts for which no law or theoretical account is yet available.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognise when a field is 'an empirical science occupied with the registration of immense numbers of disconnected facts' (chemistry examples: unexplained alloy properties, variations in iron/steel qualities). Such empirical collections have limited inferential value until they are brought under general laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accept that some empirical residue will remain
rubrics_metrics.description: We must not suppose that any science will ever entirely cease to be empirical; multitudes of phenomena remain unexplained even in advanced sciences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even well-developed theories (e.g., undulatory theory of light, electricity) leave unexplained facts (natural colours, certain electrical phenomena). Evaluations should allow for persistent empirical exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explanation as showing resemblance or general-law inclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: Every act of explanation consists in pointing out a resemblance between facts, or in showing that an observed fact is one case of a general law or tendency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good explanations connect apparently diverse phenomena by law, similarity, or identity (examples: rainbow colours explained by similarity to sunlight through a glass globe; trade winds explained by hydrostatics and Earth's rotation). Explanation 'renders a thing plain' and brings facts into harmony with other knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of explanation over mere empirical record
rubrics_metrics.description: Facts that have been explained (brought under law) are of far greater value because they admit of safe and extensive inference; mere recorded results inform only about repetition under identical circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing work, prioritise contributions that convert empirical facts into law-like explanations, since unexplained empirical facts are of 'minor value' for predicting other circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of accident in discovery (chance + preparedness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Accident often determines the moment when a new branch of knowledge is created, but the discovery depends on the reasoning power and preparedness of the observer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish mere chance events from discoveries: examples include Haüy's crystal cleavage, Malus's polarisation observation, Galvani's frog; the discoverer must have the insight and follow-up experiments to turn accident into scientific knowledge. Hence evaluate whether an author credits and analyses serendipitous observations appropriately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Systematic investigation reduces dependence on chance
rubrics_metrics.description: With the progress of science the element of chance becomes much reduced; systematic examination of phenomena leads to discoveries not fortuitous in nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value methodological thoroughness: systematic and repeated trial, broad empirical searches, and deliberate testing (e.g., systematic searches that led to chloroform evaluation) increase reliability of findings and reduce reliance on luck.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific success depends on knowledge, industry, and inference
rubrics_metrics.description: Genius united to extensive knowledge, cultivated powers, and indomitable industry constitute the characteristics of the successful discoverer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating researchers or methods, consider the practitioner's domain knowledge, persistence, and inferential skill as key predictors of discovery, beyond random chance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deduction is certain but incomplete — explore consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Deduction from a law is certain in each step, but does not guarantee that the reasoner will discover every consequence of a law; many consequences may be overlooked unless systematically pursued.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether theoretical work systematically explores and derives non-obvious consequences (examples: Hérbert's observation that light speed and Earth's motion produce stellar aberration discovered later by Bradley). Encourage thorough deductive exploration and explicit enumeration of implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prediction (prevision) is a primary test of a true theory
rubrics_metrics.description: The power to predict facts beforehand is the test of true theory; coincidence with fact and announced forecasts are convincing proofs of theory's soundness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give high weight to theories that make specific, verifiable predictions announced prior to observation (astronomy examples: eclipse and comet returns, Neptune discovery). Evaluate whether predictions were explicit and subsequently confirmed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theory's ability to predict surprising, counterintuitive phenomena
rubrics_metrics.description: A strong theory predicts complicated or singular phenomena that observation alone or analogy could not readily discover (optical examples: Fresnel's predictions, Poisson's bright spot).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing theories, look for capacity to anticipate paradoxical results later confirmed by experiment (e.g., Fresnel predicting increased illumination by a circular aperture; Poisson's point of light). Such successes are especially persuasive evidence for theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theory should guide invention of new experiments
rubrics_metrics.description: A good theory aids the invention of new experiments and suggests novel experimental arrangements that yield new phenomena.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether theoretical proposals lead to practical experimental tests or new apparatus (examples: Fresnel's use of mathematics to envisage experiments, Airy's predictions about Newton's rings). Theoretical productivity (new experiments) is a criterion of quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analogy and generalisation as explanatory tools
rubrics_metrics.description: Explanation often begins by discovery of simple resemblance; analogy and generalisation enable extension of known phenomena to new cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess use of analogy and careful generalisation (e.g., Fresnel's inference that compression could induce double refraction in transparent media). Beware overreliance on loose analogy without supporting evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theoretical precision is limited by practical complexities
rubrics_metrics.description: Even where exact theoretical treatment is possible in principle (e.g., tides for uniform ocean), irregular real-world conditions introduce complexities beyond theory's immediate reach.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge claims of prediction and explanation by accounting for environmental and boundary complexities; prefer moderated claims that recognise limitations (Whewell on tides and sea irregularities).

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross-domain verification strengthens theory
rubrics_metrics.description: Theories that account for phenomena across different domains (light, sound, tides, celestial mechanics) and whose consequences are verified in diverse contexts provide stronger confirmation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weigh multi-domain predictive success (Doppler effect in sound and light; interference phenomena across waves) as evidence of generality and robustness.
